Oliver and the Cake That Wouldn’t Wait

Oliver’s birthday cake grows two pink boots and bolts out of the kitchen. He and Pip follow it through the village, collecting a crowd along the way.

Read the whole storyMake one like this

Oliver’s story

Read the story below, or open the page-turning reader.

One suspicious hiccup.

Oliver had promised himself the cake would be finished before noon. He checked the icing, counted the candles and placed the last strawberry exactly in the centre. Pip sat beneath the table, pretending the cream did not interest him. Then the cake said, “Hic!” The strawberry jumped sideways. Oliver stared at it. Pip’s ears rose. A second hiccup shook sugar across the table. Oliver reached for the cake stand, but the sponge shifted away from his hands.

The evidence runs away.

Before Oliver could call for help, two icing-covered boots pushed through the bottom layer. The cake hopped down, tested its balance and sprinted through the open door. “That took me all morning!” Oliver shouted. Pip shot after it. Oliver grabbed his coat and followed, trying to decide which was worse: losing his birthday cake or explaining that it had escaped under its own power. At the garden gate, the cake looked back, hiccupped once and vanished into the lane.

A flour-covered witness.

The cake burst into Mrs Bell’s bakery during the lunch rush. It ducked beneath a tray of rolls. Oliver did not. Dough wrapped around his shoulders and a bowl of flour tipped over his head. By the time he stood up, Pip had become a white fox and three customers were applauding. Mrs Bell pointed towards the rear door with a wooden spoon. “It went that way,” she said. “And if it steals my oven, I’m sending you the bill.”

Travel causes trouble.

In the bookshop, pink icing led Oliver to a stack of atlases. The cake was hiding behind Europe. He moved quietly, reached between two shelves and almost caught it. An atlas snapped shut on his sleeve. The cake wriggled free, sending hardbacks flapping into the air like startled birds. Pip sneezed beneath Travel. Mr Vale peered over the counter. “Running cakes belong in Fiction,” he said. Oliver freed his arm. “At the moment, it belongs to nobody.”

An audience makes it worse.

By the time Oliver reached the market, half the village had noticed the chase. The cake bounced between vegetable stalls, clipped an orange display and caught three falling oranges on its top tier. It stopped, turned and bowed. The crowd cheered. “Please don’t encourage it,” Oliver called, though he was laughing despite himself. The cake spun again, lost one orange, caught it on the rebound and raced towards the river. Pip glanced at Oliver as if to say the cake was getting ideas.

A choice with ducks below.

The cake climbed onto the narrow wall of the old bridge. Six ducks gathered beneath it with open beaks. Oliver could rush forward and risk knocking it into the water, or wait and risk losing it again. He chose patience. One slow step. Then another. The cake leaned towards the river. Pip covered his eyes with both paws. At the last second it sprang to the far bank, scattering icing but staying upright. The ducks complained. Oliver followed, now certain the cake had somewhere to be.

The chase becomes a parade.

Beyond the bridge, the cake tore through a woodland picnic. Rabbits dropped their sandwiches. Two mice seized a napkin and ran after it. A hedgehog joined without asking why. Oliver could hear the bakers, bookseller and market crowd close behind. What had begun as a private disaster had become a noisy procession. “Nearly got you!” he called. The cake glanced back and wiggled its cherries. Pip barked once, delighted. Oliver noticed that the cake always slowed until everyone caught up.

The clue Oliver nearly missed.

At sunset, the cake reached the empty village square and stopped beneath the lanterns. Oliver skidded to a halt beside it. Mrs Bell arrived, followed by Mr Vale, the traders, rabbits, mice, one hedgehog and six deeply offended ducks. The cake turned as if checking a list. Suddenly the slowing down, the detours and the ridiculous bow made sense. “You weren’t trying to escape,” Oliver said. “You were collecting guests.” The cake gave a proud wobble. Pip looked unbearably smug.

Everyone brings something.

The journey had cost the cake most of its icing, three strawberries and one pink boot. Oliver looked at the damage, then at the crowd it had gathered. “We can fix this,” he said. Mrs Bell brought cream. The market traders opened their berry baskets. The mice returned the missing boot, slightly nibbled. Mr Vale folded paper hats from an old catalogue. Pip claimed the tallest one and appointed himself Head Taster. Oliver stopped trying to control every detail and handed out spoons.

Better than perfect.

Under the lanterns, Oliver cut the first slice. There was cake for the bakers, booksellers, traders, rabbits, mice, hedgehog and six ducks who insisted on equal portions. Pip licked cream from his nose. Around the square, people who had never spoken before traded stories about the chase. The cake gave one final, tiny “Hic!” Everyone laughed. Oliver had wanted a perfect birthday cake. What he had instead was lopsided, slightly muddy and surrounded by friends. He did not miss perfect at all.
